exact_changes.label: F5
exact_changes.text: [F5] [[thm-the-standard-flat-function-is-smooth-and-flat-at-zero]]: the function $u:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R$ given by $u(t)=\exp(-1/t)$ for $t>0$ and $u(t)=0$ for $t\le0$ is smooth on $\mathbb R$, with $u^{(m)}(0)=0$ for every $m\ge0$. The one-variable chain rule and sum, scalar-multiple and product derivative rules apply on $\mathbb R$ ([[thm-chain-rule]], [[thm-algebra-of-derivatives]]).

exact_changes.old: 1.1 Define $\chi(\omega)=e\exp(-1/(1-(\omega/\gamma)^2))$ for $|\omega|<\gamma$, and $\chi(\omega)=0$ otherwise. The exponential tends to zero faster than every power at the endpoints, so $\chi$ is real, even, smooth, compactly supported in $[-\gamma,\gamma]$, and $\chi(0)=1$.
exact_changes.new: 1.1 Let $u$ be the standard flat function of [F5] and put $q(\omega):=1-(\omega/\gamma)^2$ and $\chi(\omega):=e\,u(q(\omega))$. Since $\gamma>0$, $q$ is a smooth real polynomial. The chain and product rules in [F5], iterated at each derivative order, make $\chi$ smooth on all of $\mathbb R$: every positive-order derivative is a finite sum of products of a derivative $u^{(m)}\circ q$, with $m\ge1$, and derivatives of $q$. At $\omega=\pm\gamma$, one has $q(\omega)=0$ and every such $u^{(m)}(0)=0$, so all these derivatives vanish and match the exterior zero branch. The value itself also vanishes there because $u(0)=0$. Since $q>0$ exactly when $|\omega|<\gamma$, this formula is exactly $e\exp(-1/(1-(\omega/\gamma)^2))$ inside that interval and zero outside. Thus $\chi$ is real, even, smooth, compactly supported in $[-\gamma,\gamma]$, and $\chi(0)=e\exp(-1)=1$.

exact_changes.label: F6
exact_changes.text: [F6] [[thm-dominated-convergence]]: on a measure space, measurable complex functions converging pointwise almost everywhere and dominated in modulus by one nonnegative integrable function have convergent integrals. Apply this scalar result to each entry in a fixed finite orthonormal matrix basis; the existing Countable Choice assumption [A1] supplies the adopted Lebesgue-measure interfaces.

exact_changes.kind: replace existing DCT continuity sentence in Proof2.1
exact_changes.old: Dominated convergence, using continuity and boundedness of $H_\Lambda'(s)$ on the compact interval and the integrable majorant $2\sup_s\|H_\Lambda'(s)\||W_\gamma(t)|$, shows $D_\Lambda(s)$ is norm-continuous.
exact_changes.new: For each fixed $t$, the matrix exponential series for $e^{\pm itH_\Lambda(s)}$ converges uniformly in $s\in[0,1]$: if $M=\sup_s\|H_\Lambda(s)\|<\infty$, its order-$r$ term has norm at most $(|t|M)^r/r!$. The terms are continuous in $s$, so both exponentials, and hence their product with the continuous $H_\Lambda'(s)$, are norm-continuous in $s$. For any sequence $s_m\to s$ in $[0,1]$, each matrix entry of the difference of the filtered integrands tends pointwise to zero and has modulus at most $2\sup_v\|H_\Lambda'(v)\||W_\gamma(t)|$, an integrable majorant by step 1.1 and compact-interval boundedness of $H_\Lambda'$. The entries are measurable in $t$, since the exponentials are continuous in $t$ and $W_\gamma$ is measurable. Applying [F6] entrywise gives convergence of every entry of $D_\Lambda(s_m)-D_\Lambda(s)$. If the matrix dimension is $m_\Lambda$, then $\|R\|\le m_\Lambda\max_{i,j}|R_{ij}|$: for a unit vector $x$, $|(Rx)_i|\le\max_{i,j}|R_{ij}|\sum_j|x_j|\le\sqrt{m_\Lambda}\max_{i,j}|R_{ij}|$, and summing squares over $i$ proves the bound. Thus entrywise convergence gives norm convergence, proving norm-continuity of $D_\Lambda$ without an undeclared norm-equivalence theorem.
